answer.text: Composite attribute are mapped as it is

choices.label: B

evidence.quote: Create one relation per strong entity type, preserve its simple attributes and select a candidate key. Expand composite attributes into their useful simple components; do not copy a composite ER structure unchanged into a flat atomic design. module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF).

questions.stem: Assume atomic attribute values. Consider R(A,B,C,D) with functional dependencies F = {C→D, C→B, B→C}. Which statement about R is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The relation R is in second normal form

options.label: B
options.text: The relation R is in third normal form

options.label: C
options.text: The candidate key for R is BC

options.label: D
options.text: The relation R is in Boyce–Codd normal form

options.label: E
options.text: None of the other statements is true

questions.hint: Derive every candidate key before testing dependency-based normal forms.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 10

answer.text: None of the other statements is true
answer.explanation: Every candidate key must contain A because no dependency derives it. Both AB and AC determine all attributes and are minimal; BC determines only B, C and D. The nonprime attribute D depends on B or C alone, a proper subset of either composite key, so 2NF fails. The dependency C→D also violates 3NF and BCNF because C is not a superkey and D is nonprime. None of the other statements is true.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: False: D depends on a proper subset of a candidate key, violating 2NF.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: False: C→D has a nonsuperkey determinant and a nonprime dependent attribute, violating 3NF.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: False: (BC)+ = {B,C,D}, so BC cannot determine A and is not a key.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: False: C determines D but is not a superkey, violating BCNF.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Correct: each of the other four claims is false.

evidence.quote: For R(A,B,C,D), let C→D, C→B and B→C. A never appears on a right-hand side, so every key needs A. (AB)+ gives ABCD through B→C→D; (AC)+ also gives ABCD. AB and AC are minimal keys. BC cannot derive A and is not a key. A, B and C are prime; D is nonprime.
2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.
For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires X to be a superkey.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: A functional dependency is a constraint between two attributes or sets of attributes of entities in a database. A functional dependency is denoted by X  Y, between two sets of attributes X and Y that are subsets of relation R. The constraint is that, the values of Y component of a tuple in r depend on, or are determined by the values of X component. Alternatively, the values of X component of a tuple uniquely (or functionally) determine the values of Y component. 4.2 Types of Functional Dependency Partial Dependency - If an attribute which is not a member of the key is dependent on some part of the key (if we have composite/candidate key) then that attribute is partially functionally dependent on the key. Let {A, B} is the key set and C is no key attribute, then if {A, B} → C and [B → C or A → C] holds. We say C is partially functionally dependent on {A, B}. Partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute is functionally dependent on part of a candidate/composite key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

These Relational constraints in DBMS are derived from the rules in the system that the database represents. There are many types of Constraints in DBMS. Domain Constraints - Every domain (cell in the table or attribute value) must contain atomic values (smallest indivisible units). We perform data type check here, which means we need to assign a data type to a column and limit the values that it can contain. Key Constraints- These are called uniqueness constraints since it ensures that every tuple in the relation should be unique. An attribute that can uniquely identify a tuple in a relation is called the key or primary key of the table. The value of the attribute for different tuples in the relation has to be unique. Primary keys must be unique and cannot be null.

answer.explanation: Many-to-one means several left-side entities may share a right-side entity while each left entity has at most one right partner. Employees share departments under the stated assignment rule. Building→Location is one-to-one, Hospital→Patient is one-to-many and Author→Book is many-to-many. answer.explanation: Normalization organizes facts according to their dependencies to reduce avoidable duplication and update anomalies. That reduction is a benefit. Decomposing a table may require joins when an application needs the original combined information, which can increase retrieval cost for some workloads. Dependency analysis and schema design also take time. These are possible costs, not claims that normalization always slows a system. Declared dependencies suffice for normalization even when the current sample data shows no errors.

evidence.quote: Normalization separates facts according to their determinants, reducing avoidable repetition and associated anomalies. It does not require seeing bad current data: declared dependencies suffice. Adding a generated row ID may make insertion technically possible, but does not remove repeated facts or fix the dependency design. Reduced redundancy can improve integrity and storage use, but extra keys and joins mean neither storage savings nor faster retrieval is guaranteed.

BCNF specifically requires every nontrivial functional-dependency determinant to be a superkey.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

questions.stem:
Suppose you want to design a database for a certain company after you
know the need of all users of the database. What is the next step you are
expected to do?
questions.hint: Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable.

answer.explanation: After collecting users' information requirements, conceptual design develops the ER/EER model that represents those needs. Logical design then maps that model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Normalization refines dependency structure rather than replacing the initial conceptual modeling step. Query processing evaluates database requests instead of defining the initial enterprise model. D is therefore the next step under the stated sequence, rather than a claim that design can never iterate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: query processing evaluates requests rather than creating the initial model from requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correct: conceptual design follows the collection of requirements in the stated sequence.

evidence.quote: First collect business facts, required transactions, reports, volumes, privacy rules and quality targets. Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model. Conceptual Database Design In this phase the database designers will make a decision on the database model that perfectly suits the organization‘s requirement. The database designers will study the documents prepared by the analysis in the requirement analysis stage and then start development of a system model that fulfils the needs. Logical database design (Data model mapping) The conceptual design is translated into internal model which includes mapping of all objects i.e design of tables, indexes, views, transaction, access privileges etc. Physical Design Physical design or Database implementation needs the formation of special storage related constructs. These constructs consist of storage groups, table spaces, data files, tables etc.

questions.stem: A many to many relationship between two entities usually results in how many tables?
questions.hint: Identify relationship degree and cardinality before choosing a relational mapping.

answer.text: Three tables: two entity tables and one association table.
answer.explanation: Each of the two entity types normally has its own relation. Their many-to-many relationship requires an additional association relation holding references to both entities and any relationship attributes. FDB12 illustrates Student, Course and Enrollment. Thus the usual total is three, rather than only the one new association table.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One counts only the association table and omits the two participating entity tables.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two entity tables alone do not record arbitrary many-to-many pairs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The two entity tables plus their association table produce the usual total of three.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No fourth table is required by the ordinary binary many-to-many mapping.

evidence.quote: A binary M:N relationship needs an association table in addition to the two entity tables. Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) references Student and Course; (StudentID,CourseID) is a key if one enrollment per pair is allowed. Repeated attempts require Term or AttemptNo in the key. This ordinarily produces three tables.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Many to many (M-M) – When entities in all entity sets can take part more than once in the relationship cardinality is many to many.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 3.4 Mapping ER-models to relational tables 1. For each strong entity type E, create a relation R that includes all the attributes of E. 2. Choose one of the key attributes of E as the primary key for R. For each weak entity type W with owner entity type E (which is a strong entity), create a relation R & include all attributes of ‗W‘ as attributes of R. Also, include the primary key attribute of the relation that correspond to the owner entity type as foreign key attributes of R . 3. For each binary 1:1 relationship type R in the ER schema, identify the relations S and T that correspond to the entity types participating in R. Foreign Key approach: Choose one of the relations-say S-and include a foreign key in S the primary key of T. It is better to choose an entity type with total participation in R in the role of S. 4. For each binary 1:N relationship type R, identify the relation S that represent the participating entity type at the N-side of the relationship type. Include the primary key of the relation T as foreign key in S that represents the other entity type participating in R. Include any attributes of the 1:N relation type as attributes of S. 5. For each n-ary relationship type R, where n>2, create a new relationship S to represent R. Include the primary keys of the relations that represent the participating entity types as foreign key attributes in S. Also include any attributes of the n-ary relationship type as attributes of S.

questions.stem: An ________ is a set of entities of the same type that share the same properties, or attributes.

answer.explanation: FDB06 distinguishes an individual entity from the type describing its properties and the set containing the current entities of that type. The stem asks for that collection of similarly described entities, which is an entity set. Attributes describe properties; a model describes representation rather than the current collection itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An entity set is the collection of entities belonging to one common entity type.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An attribute set groups properties, rather than the entities possessing those properties.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Relation set is not the ER term for the stated collection of entities.

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: An entity is a distinguishable real or conceptual thing, such as one student or one course. An entity type describes common properties; its current collection of entities is an entity set. A relationship associates entities. Key Super Key − A set of attributes (one or more) that collectively identifies an entity in an entity set. Candidate Key − A minimal super key is called a candidate key. module_refs.quote: An entity may be an object with a physical existence (for example, a particular person, car, house, or employee) or it may be an object with a conceptual existence (for instance, a company, a job, or a university course). In ER diagrams, an entity is placed in a rectangle. Each entity has attributes, the particular properties that describe it. Entities that do not have key attributes of their own are called weak entity. The regular entity types that have a key attribute are called strong entity types. questions.stem: E-R modeling technique is a :
questions.hint: Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable.

answer.text: Top-down is the usual conceptual ER approach.
answer.explanation: FDB05 describes conceptual design as usually starting with an enterprise view and working downward into entity and relationship details. This is the usual top-down classification of ER modeling. Bottom-up refinement is associated here with normalization from dependencies. This is a useful conventional approach, rather than a claim that every ER modeling activity must follow one direction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Conceptual ER modeling usually moves from an overall enterprise view toward detailed entities and relationships.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bottom-up dependency refinement describes normalization here, rather than the usual ER conceptual approach.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Left-right is not a database design methodology identified here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Top-down is an available and appropriate description of the usual conceptual ER approach.

evidence.quote: First collect business facts, required transactions, reports, volumes, privacy rules and quality targets. Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model. Logical design maps the conceptual model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Physical design chooses file organization, indexes and storage. Implementation creates and loads the actual objects; testing checks requirements.
Conceptual design usually proceeds from a whole enterprise view downward; normalization can refine structures from dependencies upward.
These are useful approaches rather than mandatory directions for every modeling activity.

module_refs.quote: 3.1 Database Modeling High-level conceptual data models provide concepts for presenting data in ways that are close to the way people perceive data. A typical example is the entity relationship model, which uses main concepts like entities, attributes and relationships.

It is a modeling tool used to depict graphically a DB design before it is actually implemented. It shows the various entities being modeled and the important relationships among them. ERD has three basic components Entity, Relationship and Attribute.

questions.stem: The number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set is expressed as :
questions.hint: Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints.

answer.explanation: Cardinality measures how often an entity participates and distinguishes one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many. That is the number of possible associations asked about.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Entity is a participating object. (PDF pp. 11, 12.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cardinality is the association-count constraint. (PDF pp. 11, 12.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Schema describes structure rather than the count. (PDF pp. 11, 12.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Attributes are properties, not the association-count classification. (PDF pp. 11, 12.)

evidence.quote: Cardinality specifies maximum associated occurrences: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. Minimum cardinality specifies optional/partial participation (zero permitted) or mandatory/total participation (at least one). A maximum of one does not mean participation is compulsory. Relationship degree counts participating entity roles: unary recursive, binary or ternary.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Cardinality The number of times an entity of an entity set participates in a relationship set is known as cardinality. Cardinality can be of different types: One to one (1-1) – When each entity in each entity set can take part only once in the relationship, the cardinality is one to one. One to many(1-M)– When entities in one entity set can take part only once in the relationship set and entities in other entity set can take part more than once in the relationship set, cardinality is many to one.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Many to many (M-M) – When entities in all entity sets can take part more than once in the relationship cardinality is many to many. The participation constraint specifies whether the existence of an entity depends on its being related to another entity via the relationship type. This constraint specifies the minimum number of relationship instances that each entity can participate in and is sometimes called the minimum cardinality constraint. There are two types of participation constraints, total and partial.

questions.stem: Relations produced from an E-R model will always be in :
questions.hint: Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order.

answer.text: First normal form, assuming correct ER-to-relational mapping.
answer.explanation: FDB20 states that properly splitting composite and multivalued ER structures produces ordinary 1NF relations. Nothing in an ER drawing alone proves absence of partial, transitive or multivalued dependencies needed for higher forms. Thus A is the guaranteed level under correct relational mapping; the word always must not be read as excusing an incorrect mapping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Correctly mapped atomic relations are in 1NF; this is the guaranteed level described here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ER model alone does not rule out partial dependencies on a composite candidate key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ER model alone does not establish the full dependency conditions required for 3NF.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ER model alone does not rule out the nontrivial multivalued dependencies addressed by 4NF.

evidence.quote: 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen relational domains and no repeating groups in cells. It does not mean merely declaring a primary key. A mapped ER design that correctly splits composite and multivalued structures gives ordinary 1NF tables; ER drawing alone guarantees no higher form.
Higher forms inherit 2NF, so no partial dependencies establishes the minimum guaranteed stage only when 1NF is also assumed.
A relation whose every candidate key is single-attribute has no nonprime partial-key dependency.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

questions.stem: In ER model the details of the entities are hidden from the user. This process is called :
questions.hint: Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects.

answer.explanation: Abstraction hides unwanted or irrelevant details. Generalization groups subclasses; specialization divides a superclass. Thus hiding entity details describes abstraction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Generalization combines common characteristics, rather than the general detail-hiding process. (PDF pp. 6, 13.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Specialization separates narrower classes. (PDF pp. 6, 13.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abstraction is explicitly the process of hiding details. (PDF pp. 6, 13.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The required term is present. (PDF pp. 6, 13.)

evidence.quote: The external level gives each user group a selected view. The conceptual level describes the whole logical database: entity types, relationships, data types and constraints. The internal/physical level describes files, record placement and access paths. These are abstraction levels, distinct from client/server deployment tiers.
Specialization divides Student into Undergraduate and Graduate; generalization combines common properties into Student.
EER extends ER with superclass/subclass structure.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Data abstraction and Insulation between programs and data- Data Abstraction is a process of hiding unwanted or irrelevant details from the end user. It provides a different view and helps in achieving data independence which is used to enhance the security of data.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Specialization is the process of dividing a parent-level entity (super-class) into narrower categories (sub-classes) accordingly to all the possible child categories. Specialization requires the separation of entities based on certain uncommon attributes. The process of extracting common characteristics from two or more classes (sub-classes) and combining them into a generalized superclass is called Generalization. It is the process that does the grouping entities into broader or distributed categories based on certain common attributes.

questions.stem: The attributes made up of more than one single attributes are called
questions.hint: Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model.

answer.explanation: Composite attributes have smaller meaningful subparts. This differs from multiple values of one attribute and from calculating a value from another.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Composite is the stated divisible structure. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Derived concerns computation from stored attributes. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Single-valued concerns count of values, not internal composition. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multivalued concerns a set of values rather than components of one value. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

evidence.quote: Simple versus composite asks whether a value has meaningful components: Address may split into City and Street. Single-valued versus multivalued asks how many values one entity may have: a student may have several phone numbers. These dimensions differ: one address may be composite and single-valued. Age derived from birth date is derived, even if also single-valued. Attribute names alone do not establish multiplicity.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Composite and Simple (Atomic) Attributes Composite attributes can be divided into smaller subparts, which represent more basic attributes with independent meanings. Attributes that are not divisible are called simple or atomic attributes. Multivalued Attributes Most attributes have a single value for a particular entity; such attributes are called single-valued. For example, Age is a single-valued attribute of a person. In some cases an attribute can have a set of values for the same entity. For instance, a College_degrees attribute for a person. Similarly, one person may not have any college degrees, another person may have one, and a third person may have two or more degrees; therefore, different people can have different numbers of values for the College_degrees attribute. Such attributes are called multivalued.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Derived Attributes In some cases, two (or more) attribute values are related. For example, the Age and Birth_date attributes of a person. For a particular person entity, the value of Age can be determined from the current (today‘s) date and the value of that person‘s Birth_date. The Age attribute is hence called a derived attribute and is said to be derivable from the Birth_date attribute, which is called a stored attribute.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 4.3 Database Anomalies Database Anomalies are the flaws in databases which occurs because of poor database design and storing everything in a single flat database. They are problems that are caused usually by redundant data. Types of database anomalies are Insertion anomaly, Deletion anomaly, and Update anomaly. Insertion Anomaly - occurs when the entire primary key is not known and the database cannot insert a new record properly. This would violate entity integrity. It can be avoided by using a sequence number for the primary key. Deletion Anomaly - happens when a record is deleted that results in the loss of other related data. It can be avoided by normalizing tables in a database to minimize their dependency. Update Anomaly - occurs when a change to one attribute value causes the database to either contain inconsistent data or causes multiple records to need changing. It may be prevented by making sure tables are in third normal form.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

answer.explanation: First normal form is the first stage requiring atomic values and no repeating groups in cells. It does not by itself remove partial or transitive functional dependencies. Second normal form adds the full-dependency condition, third normal form adds the determinant/prime-attribute rule, and BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. These stronger forms inherit atomicity, but the question asks for the first stage defining it.

choices.explanation: Incorrect: 2NF inherits atomicity and additionally excludes nonprime partial dependencies; it is a later stage.

choices.label: B

For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires X to be a superkey. The mnemonic whole key and nothing but the key describes the common single-key case; it cannot replace the full tests when keys overlap. Remove dependencies of nonprime facts on nonkey determinants.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

questions.stem: A relation has atomic values with no repeating groups, and no nonprime attribute partially depends on any candidate key. What is the strongest normal form guaranteed by these facts alone?
questions.hint: Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order.
sources: Computer Science model exam collection · Question 40

answer.explanation: Atomic values without repeating groups establish 1NF. Adding the absence of nonprime partial dependencies establishes 2NF. Higher normal forms have additional requirements involving nonkey determinants or multivalued dependencies, and none of those requirements follows from the stated facts. Thus 2NF is the strongest guaranteed level, even though the relation could also happen to satisfy higher forms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No restriction on nontrivial multivalued dependencies has been established.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 1NF plus the absence of nonprime partial dependencies guarantees 2NF.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 1NF holds, but 2NF is the stronger guarantee.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 3NF requires additional determinant/prime-attribute conditions.

evidence.quote: 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen relational domains and no repeating groups in cells. It does not mean merely declaring a primary key. A mapped ER design that correctly splits composite and multivalued structures gives ordinary 1NF tables; ER drawing alone guarantees no higher form.
2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.
Higher forms inherit 2NF, so no partial dependencies establishes the minimum guaranteed stage only when 1NF is also assumed.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

Conceptual Database Design In this phase the database designers will make a decision on the database model that perfectly suits the organization‘s requirement. The database designers will study the documents prepared by the analysis in the requirement analysis stage and then start development of a system model that fulfils the needs. Logical database design (Data model mapping) The conceptual design is translated into internal model which includes mapping of all objects i.e design of tables, indexes, views, transaction, access privileges etc. Physical Design Physical design or Database implementation needs the formation of special storage related constructs. These constructs consist of storage groups, table spaces, data files, tables etc.

choices.explanation: Incorrect: 3NF inherits 2NF and imposes its additional determinant/prime-attribute condition; it is not the first stage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey; it is stronger than the first stage imposing the partial-dependency rule.

evidence.quote: 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen relational domains and no repeating groups in cells.
2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.

For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires X to be a superkey. The mnemonic whole key and nothing but the key describes the common single-key case; it cannot replace the full tests when keys overlap. Remove dependencies of nonprime facts on nonkey determinants.

A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.

questions.stem: What defines a composite key in database design?

options.label: A
options.text: A key made up of two or more attributes

options.label: B
options.text: A foreign key that references multiple tables

options.label: C
options.text: A unique identifier for a column in a table

options.label: D
options.text: A key used for data encryption

questions.hint: Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 135

answer.text: A. A key made up of two or more attributes
answer.explanation: Composite describes the number of attributes in a key: it contains two or more attributes. It does not mean the key has necessarily been selected as the primary key, nor does it refer to the number of tables reached by a reference. A column name alone is not a multicolumn identification key. Encryption uses a different meaning of key.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two or more key attributes are the defining feature.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The number of referenced tables does not define composition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A column identifier does not describe a multicolumn key.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An encryption key is a different concept.

evidence.quote: A superkey uniquely identifies a tuple. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any component loses uniqueness. Minimal means no unnecessary attribute, not necessarily the fewest columns among all keys. A primary key is one selected candidate key; remaining candidates are alternate keys. A composite key contains multiple attributes and need not be the chosen primary key.
A composite-key example must include multiple columns; a single-column key is not composite.
A table can have several candidates and foreign keys but at most one declared primary-key constraint, possibly containing several columns.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Partial Dependency - If an attribute which is not a member of the key is dependent on some part of the key (if we have composite/candidate key) then that attribute is partially functionally dependent on the key. Let {A, B} is the key set and C is no key attribute, then if {A, B} → C and [B → C or A → C] holds. We say C is partially functionally dependent on {A, B}. Partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute is functionally dependent on part of a candidate/composite key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Super Key − A set of attributes (one or more) that collectively identifies an entity in an entity set. Candidate Key − A minimal super key is called a candidate key. An entity set may have more than one candidate key. Primary Key − A primary key is one of the candidate keys chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify the entity set.

answer.explanation: Indexes are auxiliary structures used to speed retrieval for search conditions, rather than stored binary values or security mechanisms.

choices.label: B

answer.explanation: A data dictionary describes the database rather than serving as ordinary application data storage. choices.label: B

answer.explanation: Uniqueness constrains distinct tuple identifiers, whereas SELECT, INSERT and DELETE are language operations in the DML list. UNIQUE is the offered constraint name matching that property.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of referential integrity in a database?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent unauthorized access to data

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure data consistency and integrity across related tables

sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 139
Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 154

answer.text: To ensure data consistency and integrity across related tables
answer.explanation: Referential integrity maintains consistency between related tuples by requiring non-null child references to resolve to existing parent keys. It controls valid relationships rather than authorization, performance, or encoding.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unauthorized access is a security issue. (PDF pp. 14, 48.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Matches the module's consistency-between-relations definition. (PDF pp. 14, 48.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Query performance is not the referential validity rule. (PDF pp. 14, 48.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encryption is a separate security mechanism. (PDF pp. 14, 48.)

evidence.quote: Domain integrity restricts type and allowed values. Key integrity enforces uniqueness. Entity integrity requires every primary-key component to be non-NULL. Referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign-key value to match an eligible referenced unique/candidate key; self-references are allowed. A parent need not have a child.
Both encryption and access control can protect patient data.
Authentication verifies identity; role-based authorization limits allowed records/actions; encryption protects data at rest or in transit; auditing records activity.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Referential Integrity Constraints - The Referential integrity constraints is specified between two relations or tables and used to maintain the consistency among the tuples in two relations. questions.stem: What is denormalization in database design?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of breaking down a complex table into smaller tables

options.label: B
options.text: The process of adding redundancy to improve data retrieval performance

options.label: C
options.text: The process of eliminating duplicate values from a table

options.label: D
options.text: The process of converting data into a different format for storage

answer.text: Deliberately adding redundancy to improve selected retrieval workloads.
answer.explanation: FDB38 defines denormalization as deliberately repeating or precomputing facts to reduce selected read costs, with extra maintenance work. It is a workload-driven trade-off rather than elimination of all duplication. Breaking tables apart typically describes normalization; changing storage format is a different concern. Thus B captures both the mechanism and its intended retrieval benefit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Splitting tables according to dependencies is normalization, rather than the redundancy introduced by denormalization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Denormalization deliberately repeats or precomputes information to improve selected retrieval workloads.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Eliminating duplication describes a different direction from deliberately introducing useful redundant facts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Changing storage format does not define the dependency and redundancy trade-off of denormalization.

evidence.quote: Normalization reduces dependency-driven anomalies. Indexing supplies search paths. answer.explanation: FDB02 says object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior. That matches a collection of objects directly. The other choices have different defining structures: a hierarchical model uses a parent–child tree, a classic network model uses pointer-based owner/member links, and an object model uses objects with identity, state and behavior. Products may combine features, but the question asks for the model defined by rows and columns, which is relational.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: the hierarchical model organizes records in a parent–child tree.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct: the relational model uses relations represented as tables of rows and columns.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: the object model represents objects with identity, state and behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: the classic network model uses pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents.

evidence.quote: A data model supplies concepts for structure, relationships, constraints and operations. Conceptual ER models describe entities and relationships. Relational models use tables; hierarchical models organize records in a parent–child tree; classic network models connect records through pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents. Object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior. A physical model specifies record layouts and access paths. These are different representation choices, not stages of one query.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 3.6 The Relational Database Model The relational model represents the database as a collection of relations. A table is represented with columns and rows. Each table is an entity in the ER diagram. Each row is known as a tuple. Each table of the column has a name or attribute of the entity. 3.7 Relational Model Concepts in DBMS Attribute: Each column in a Table. Attributes are the properties which define a relation Tables – In the Relational model, relations are saved in the table format. It is stored along with its entities. A table has two properties rows and columns. Rows represent records and columns represent attributes. Tuple – It is a single row of a table, which contains a single record.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a database schema?

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: To define the structure and organization of a database

questions.hint: Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 147

answer.text: To define the structure and organization of a database
answer.explanation: A schema is the database description specified during design. It expresses structure, types, relationships and constraints; enforcing a particular constraint is narrower than the description's overall purpose.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Types are included, but enforcement alone is narrower than the schema description. (PDF pp. 7, 7.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Files hold data physically; the schema describes the database. (PDF pp. 7, 7.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Structure and organization match the schema definition. (PDF pp. 7, 7.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Integrity conditions can be specified in a schema, but integrity alone is not its overall descriptive purpose. (PDF pp. 7, 7.)

evidence.quote: A schema describes names, structures and constraints; an instance, state or snapshot is the data at a particular time. Inserting a student changes the state, while adding a column changes the schema. Metadata is data describing data. The catalog or data dictionary records table definitions, types, constraints and often access privileges and optimizer statistics. A schema diagram draws tables and key references; labels such as database diagram can overlap.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: A data model a collection of concepts that can be used to describe the structure of a database and provides the necessary means to achieve data abstraction. By structure of a database we mean the data types, relationships, and constraints that apply to the data. Most data models also include a set of basic operations for specifying retrievals and updates on the database.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 2.2 Schemas and Instances The description of a database is called the database schema, which is specified during database design and is not expected to change frequently. The data in the database at a particular moment of time is called a database state or snapshot. It is also called the current set of occurrences or instances in the database.

questions.stem: What is the role of a database administrator (DBA) in database management?

options.label: A

answer.text: To manage and maintain the database system
answer.explanation: The DBA administers database and DBMS resources, authorizes access and coordinates/monitors use. Management and maintenance summarize those system responsibilities.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

In a database environment, the primary resource is the database itself, and the secondary resource is the DBMS and related software. Administering these resources is the responsibility of the database administrator (DBA). Which database model represents data as a hierarchical structure with parent-child
relationships?

answer.explanation: The defining phrase is a hierarchical parent-child structure. FDB02 assigns that tree organization to the hierarchical model. The relational model uses tables; the object model represents identity, state and behavior; the network model permits more general links including multiple parents. A parent-child tree therefore selects A directly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The hierarchical model organizes records into a parent-child tree.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The relational model represents data as tables rather than a prescribed parent-child tree.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The object model represents object identity, state and behavior rather than requiring a tree.

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: A data model supplies concepts for structure, relationships, constraints and operations. Conceptual ER models describe entities and relationships. Relational models use tables; hierarchical models organize records in a parent–child tree; classic network models connect records through pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents. Object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior. A physical model specifies record layouts and access paths. These are different representation choices, not stages of one query.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Types of Data Models 1. High-level or conceptual data models provide concepts that are close to the way many users perceive data. Entity – Relationship (E/R) model and Object-Oriented Model are examples of conceptual/high level data model. 2. Low-level or physical data models provide concepts that describe the details of how data is stored on the computer storage media. Concepts provided by physical data models are generally meant for computer specialists, not for end users. 3. representational (or implementation) data model provides concepts that may be easily understood by end users but that are not too far from the way data is organized in computer storage. Representational data models hide many details of data storage on disk but can be implemented on a computer system directly. The widely used relational data models are the network and hierarchical.

questions.stem: What is the first step in the database design process?
questions.hint: Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 150

answer.explanation: The initial design step is to understand the organization's information needs, required transactions, reports and constraints. Those requirements guide conceptual modeling, which is then mapped into a logical schema. Defining table relationships and determining the schema therefore depend on the earlier analysis. Queries express required operations against a model rather than replacing the initial work of identifying what information and behavior are needed. C is the first step in that sequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: table relationships are designed to satisfy requirements already identified.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incorrect: schema choices follow the analysis of required information and operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct: analyze information requirements before choosing the model and schema.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: query construction depends on understanding the required information and intended database structure.

evidence.quote: First collect business facts, required transactions, reports, volumes, privacy rules and quality targets. Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model. Logical design maps the conceptual model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Physical design chooses file organization, indexes and storage. Implementation creates and loads the actual objects; testing checks requirements.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 3.2 Phases of database design The phases of database development life cycle (DDLC) in the Database Management System (DBMS) are explained below. Requirement Analysis The most important step in implementing a database system is to find out what is needed i.e what type of a database is required for the business organization, daily volume of data, how much data needs to be stored in the master files etc. In order to collect all this information, a database analyst spends a lot of time within the business organization talking to people, end users and getting acquainted with the day-to-day process. Conceptual Database Design In this phase the database designers will make a decision on the database model that perfectly suits the organization‘s requirement. The database designers will study the documents prepared by the analysis in the requirement analysis stage and then start development of a system model that fulfils the needs.

questions.stem: Read pairs left→right. Student↔Course and Product↔Supplier permit many occurrences in both directions. Each employee belongs to one department with many employees. Each order belongs to one customer, who may place many orders. Which pair is one-to-many?
questions.hint: Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 151

answer.explanation: Customer→Order is one-to-many because one customer can place several orders and each order belongs to one customer. Employee→Department runs in the opposite direction: many employees share one department, making it many-to-one. The student/course and product/supplier pairs explicitly permit many partners in both directions and are many-to-many. Cardinality follows these rules and the direction of the pair.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Student→Course is M:N under the stated enrollment rule.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Employee→Department is N:1.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Customer→Order is 1:N under the ownership rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Product→Supplier is M:N under the stated supply rule.

evidence.quote: Cardinality specifies maximum associated occurrences: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. Minimum cardinality specifies optional/partial participation (zero permitted) or mandatory/total participation (at least one). A maximum of one does not mean participation is compulsory. Relationship degree counts participating entity roles: unary recursive, binary or ternary.
If each employee belongs to one department and each department has many employees, Employee→Department is N:1; Department→Employee is 1:N.
Read business rules in both directions.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Cardinality The number of times an entity of an entity set participates in a relationship set is known as cardinality. Cardinality can be of different types: One to one (1-1) – When each entity in each entity set can take part only once in the relationship, the cardinality is one to one. One to many(1-M)– When entities in one entity set can take part only once in the relationship set and entities in other entity set can take part more than once in the relationship set, cardinality is many to one.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Many to many (M-M) – When entities in all entity sets can take part more than once in the relationship cardinality is many to many.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of using database indexes?
questions.hint: Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 153

answer.explanation: The auxiliary index provides alternative access paths to speed retrieval under search conditions. This is the directly supported benefit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Redundancy is not the benefit identified by the index definition. (PDF pp. 21.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reduced integrity is not a stated benefit. (PDF pp. 21.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Retrieval improvement is explicitly stated. (PDF pp. 21.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Simplification of the logical model is not the index's stated function. (PDF pp. 21.)

evidence.quote: An index stores search keys with pointers or row identifiers. It often speeds selective retrieval but consumes space and must be maintained on writes. A full scan can win for a tiny table or a query returning most rows. Indexes do not themselves establish referential integrity.
Secondary indexes provide other access paths and must represent all searchable values with record pointers or pointer lists.
A dense index represents each search value; sparse indexes rely on ordered data between entries.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 5.5 Index Indexes are additional auxiliary access structures which are used to speed up the retrieval of records in response to certain search conditions. questions.stem: Employee has required, unique SSN and Employee ID values. Names and salaries may repeat. Which listed individual attributes are candidate keys? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 155

answer.text: A. Social Security Number (SSN); C. Employee ID
answer.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set guaranteed to identify a tuple. Each required unique single-attribute identifier is already minimal, so SSN and Employee ID both qualify. Names and salaries may repeat and therefore cannot guarantee identification. The question asks for candidate keys rather than the one candidate later selected as the primary key, allowing both identifiers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Required unique SSN identifies each employee and is minimal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated names are permitted, so Name is not a candidate key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Required unique Employee ID independently identifies each employee.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Repeated salaries are permitted, so Salary is not a candidate key.

evidence.quote: A superkey uniquely identifies a tuple. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any component loses uniqueness. Minimal means no unnecessary attribute, not necessarily the fewest columns among all keys. A primary key is one selected candidate key; remaining candidates are alternate keys. A composite key contains multiple attributes and need not be the chosen primary key.
If ID is unique, both {ID} and {ID,City} are superkeys, but only {ID} is minimal.
Prefer stable, compact identifiers when practical, but Email, SSN or EmployeeID is a candidate only if business rules guarantee uniqueness.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Super Key − A set of attributes (one or more) that collectively identifies an entity in an entity set. Candidate Key − A minimal super key is called a candidate key. An entity set may have more than one candidate key. Primary Key − A primary key is one of the candidate keys chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify the entity set.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a foreign key in database design?

options.label: A
options.text: To enforce data types in columns

questions.hint: Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 156

answer.explanation: A foreign key links a child occurrence to the matching parent candidate/primary key. Its defining purpose is the intertable relationship.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Domain constraints specify legal types. (PDF pp. 48.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The parent key is an identifying constraint, while the child FK expresses the reference. (PDF pp. 48.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Matches the stated linking purpose. (PDF pp. 48.)

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: Domain integrity restricts type and allowed values. Key integrity enforces uniqueness. Entity integrity requires every primary-key component to be non-NULL. Referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign-key value to match an eligible referenced unique/candidate key; self-references are allowed. A parent need not have a child.
A primary key is one selected candidate key; remaining candidates are alternate keys.
A composite key contains multiple attributes and need not be the chosen primary key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: iv. Referential Integrity ⚫ A ―foreign key‖ links each occurrence in a relation representing a child entity to the occurrence of the parent entity containing the matching candidate (usually primary) key ⚫ Referential Integrity means that if the foreign key contains a value, that value must refer to an existing occurrence in the parent entity

questions.stem: Which of the following database design principles promotes data independence?
questions.hint: Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 157

answer.explanation: Abstraction hides irrelevant details and helps achieve data independence. Three-schema separation then permits changes at one level without forcing higher-level schema changes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ER modeling describes conceptual structure but is not the explicit independence principle here. (PDF pp. 6, 8.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Normalization addresses redundancy/anomalies. (PDF pp. 6, 8.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Indexes address retrieval paths and performance. (PDF pp. 6, 8.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Abstraction is explicitly connected to independence. (PDF pp. 6, 8.)

evidence.quote: Physical data independence permits changing internal storage without changing the conceptual schema, for example adding an index. Logical data independence permits conceptual changes while preserving affected external views and application interfaces, for example splitting a table while maintaining a compatible view. It is harder because applications depend on logical meaning. Data abstraction hides irrelevant details; program–data insulation separates data definitions from application code.
Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model.
Logical design maps the conceptual model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Data abstraction and Insulation between programs and data- Data Abstraction is a process of hiding unwanted or irrelevant details from the end user. It provides a different view and helps in achieving data independence which is used to enhance the security of data.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 2.4 Data Independence The three-schema architecture can be used to further explain the concept of data independence, which can be defined as the capacity to change the schema at one level of a database system without having to change the schema at the next higher level. The two types of data independence: 1. Logical data independence is the capacity to change the conceptual schema without having to change external schemas or application programs. 2. Physical data independence is the capacity to change the internal schema without having to change the conceptual schema. Hence, the external schemas do not need be changed as well.

questions.stem: Which type of database relationship is represented by a join table?
questions.hint: Identify relationship degree and cardinality before choosing a relational mapping.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 158

answer.explanation: A join table stores pairs of references to the two participating entity tables, optionally with relationship attributes. FDB12 uses Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) for the many-to-many Student–Course relationship. One-to-one and one-to-many relationships normally use a foreign key in an entity table instead. A hierarchy is a structural pattern, not the relationship cardinality represented by this usual association mapping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A 1:1 relationship normally uses a UNIQUE foreign key rather than requiring a join table.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A 1:N relationship normally stores the one-side key in the many-side entity table.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A join or association table stores the pairs making up a many-to-many relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hierarchical organization is not the standard cardinality category represented by this association-table mapping.

evidence.quote: A binary M:N relationship needs an association table in addition to the two entity tables. Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) references Student and Course; (StudentID,CourseID) is a key if one enrollment per pair is allowed. Repeated attempts require Term or AttemptNo in the key. This ordinarily produces three tables.
For 1:N, place the one-side key as a foreign key in the many-side table; store relationship attributes there.
For 1:1, one side may hold the other key with a UNIQUE constraint.

module_refs.quote: Many to many (M-M) – When entities in all entity sets can take part more than once in the relationship cardinality is many to many.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: 3.4 Mapping ER-models to relational tables 1. For each strong entity type E, create a relation R that includes all the attributes of E. 2. Choose one of the key attributes of E as the primary key for R. For each weak entity type W with owner entity type E (which is a strong entity), create a relation R & include all attributes of ‗W‘ as attributes of R. Also, include the primary key attribute of the relation that correspond to the owner entity type as foreign key attributes of R . 3. For each binary 1:1 relationship type R in the ER schema, identify the relations S and T that correspond to the entity types participating in R. Foreign Key approach: Choose one of the relations-say S-and include a foreign key in S the primary key of T. It is better to choose an entity type with total participation in R in the role of S. 4. For each binary 1:N relationship type R, identify the relation S that represent the participating entity type at the N-side of the relationship type. Include the primary key of the relation T as foreign key in S that represents the other entity type participating in R. Include any attributes of the 1:N relation type as attributes of S. 5. For each n-ary relationship type R, where n>2, create a new relationship S to represent R. Include the primary keys of the relations that represent the participating entity types as foreign key attributes in S. Also include any attributes of the n-ary relationship type as attributes of S.

questions.stem: Employee ID uniquely identifies an employee and their name, salary and department. Names may repeat; the same salary may occur in different departments, and a department may contain different salaries. Which listed functional dependency is guaranteed?
questions.hint: Compute closures using the declared dependencies and test minimality.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 159

answer.explanation: A functional dependency is guaranteed by business rules for every legal state. Unique Employee ID determines all employee attributes, including Name, so A follows. Repeated names can correspond to different IDs, equal salaries can occur in different departments, and one department may contain different salaries. Those permissions prevent the other proposed directions from being guaranteed dependencies.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The unique employee identifier determines the employee's name.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated names can belong to different IDs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The same salary may occur in different departments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One department may contain employees with different salaries.

evidence.quote: X→Y means every legal pair of tuples agreeing on X also agrees on Y. It is a business constraint, not a correlation observed in one sample. Full dependency requires all determinant attributes; partial dependency holds through a proper subset. A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key; a nonprime attribute belongs to none.
Remove attributes and recompute to test minimality.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: A functional dependency is a constraint between two attributes or sets of attributes of entities in a database. A functional dependency is denoted by X  Y, between two sets of attributes X and Y that are subsets of relation R. The constraint is that, the values of Y component of a tuple in r depend on, or are determined by the values of X component. Alternatively, the values of X component of a tuple uniquely (or functionally) determine the values of Y component.

questions.stem: Compared with scanning all pages of a large heap file, which advantage can an RDBMS with a suitable index provide for a query selecting a small fraction of rows? Assume index lookup costs less than the scan.
questions.hint: Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 161

answer.explanation: The suitable index provides a search path for the selective query, reducing the work compared with scanning the large heap under the stated cost assumption. This supports faster retrieval for this workload. It does not remove normalization concerns, guarantee smaller storage or establish external-system compatibility. Index space and maintenance costs remain separate trade-offs from the query's retrieval advantage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: External integration is outside the stated lookup comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Indexes consume additional storage rather than guaranteeing a reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An index does not remove the need for dependency-aware design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stated cheaper indexed lookup supports faster retrieval for this query.

evidence.quote: Normalization reduces dependency-driven anomalies. Indexing supplies search paths. Denormalization deliberately repeats or precomputes facts to reduce selected read costs, increasing maintenance work. Partitioning divides rows or columns; replication creates copies to improve locality or availability while complicating updates. These techniques can coexist. An e-commerce or gaming label alone does not select one.
It often speeds selective retrieval but consumes space and must be maintained on writes.
A full scan can win for a tiny table or a query returning most rows.

questions.stem: Which normal forms have defining restrictions on functional dependencies? Select all that apply. Treat 1NF as the atomic-value/no-repeating-groups requirement.
questions.hint: Test determinants and prime attributes against the stated normal-form rules.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 165

answer.text: B. Second Normal Form (2NF); C. Third Normal Form (3NF); D. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
answer.explanation: Second normal form excludes nonprime partial functional dependencies on candidate keys. Third normal form checks each nontrivial dependency using the determinant's superkey status or the dependent's prime status. BCNF strengthens that test by requiring a superkey determinant. These three therefore use functional-dependency restrictions. First normal form instead establishes the atomic-value foundation and absence of repeating groups.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 1NF addresses atomic values and repeating groups rather than the stated dependency-based tests.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 2NF is defined through absence of nonprime partial functional dependencies on candidate keys.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 3NF tests nontrivial FDs using determinant superkeys and prime dependent attributes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: BCNF requires every nontrivial FD determinant to be a superkey.

evidence.quote: For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires X to be a superkey. The mnemonic whole key and nothing but the key describes the common single-key case; it cannot replace the full tests when keys overlap. Remove dependencies of nonprime facts on nonkey determinants.
A relation whose every candidate key is single-attribute has no nonprime partial-key dependency.
2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: First normal form (1NF) A relation (table) R is in 1NF if and only if (iff) all underlying domains of attributes contain only atomic (simple or indivisible) values. i.e. The value of any attribute in a tuple (row) must be a single value from the domain of their attribute. It is defined to disallow multivalued attributes, composite attributes, and their combinations. In other words, 1NF disallows relations within relations or relations as attribute values within tuples. It must be remove repeating groups (values) in a single field. The primary key with repeating group attributes are moved into a new table. When a relation contains no repeating groups (values), it is in first normal form (1NF). Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form (2NF) is based on the concept of full functional dependency. A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (i.e. the non-prime attributes are not partially dependent on key attributes). Remove any partially dependent attributes and place them in another relation. A partial dependency is when the attribute(s) is/are dependent on a part of a key.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote: Third Normal Form (3NF) A relation schema R is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute of ‗R‘ are fully functionally dependent on every key of R and non-transitively dependent on every key of R.
